name: Test booster blends (Prime Male, TestoFuel)

card.summary: Multi-herb over-the-counter testosterone-booster products; no published trial of these specific products was found.
card.note: Individual herbal ingredients such as Tribulus have not consistently affected testosterone in controlled studies.

quick.overview:
Test booster blends are over-the-counter supplements that combine several herbs, vitamins and minerals and are marketed to raise or support testosterone. Prime Male and TestoFuel are two brands discussed in these communities.

No published clinical trial of either named product was found. The research that exists concerns individual ingredients, and the sources reviewed describe it as inconsistent.
quick.mechanism: Marketing generally says the ingredients support the body's own testosterone production or reduce its conversion or binding. The sources reviewed do not describe the formulations of either brand, so mechanisms are not assessed here. For one common ingredient, Tribulus terrestris, Wikipedia states that it did not consistently affect testosterone levels in controlled studies [1].
quick.risks: Supplement blends are sold without prior approval for effectiveness. The Australian Institute of Sport, cited by Wikipedia, discourages athletes from using Tribulus supplements, citing no good evidence of effectiveness or safety [1]. Ingredient lists and interactions vary by product.

lead: Test booster blends are multi-ingredient dietary supplements marketed to increase or support testosterone, usually combining herbal extracts, vitamins and minerals. Brands such as Prime Male and TestoFuel are sold online and are discussed in forums on testosterone and looksmaxxing.

No published clinical trial of Prime Male or TestoFuel was found. Research on single ingredients is inconsistent; for example, Wikipedia states that Tribulus terrestris did not consistently affect testosterone levels in controlled studies and that high-quality research has not been conducted [1].

paras: Blends differ by brand. Because product formulations are set by the manufacturers and change over time, readers should consult current product labels for ingredients. The best-known ingredient with a Wikipedia article is Tribulus terrestris, which has been used in supplements since the 1980s on the belief that it raises testosterone [1].
No studies found of Prime Male or TestoFuel as products.
For context on one ingredient, Wikipedia reports that T. terrestris did not consistently affect testosterone in controlled studies and that no reviews show strength-enhancing effects [1].

The brands are discussed on testosterone-focused forums, where members ask for natural and inexpensive ways to raise testosterone. Forum material available for this article was too thin to summarise further. The Australian Institute of Sport discourages athletes from using Tribulus supplements, citing no good evidence for effectiveness or safety [1].
